title: Cubital Fossa Topography and Elbow Ligamentous Anatomy

steps.tx: The **cubital fossa** is a triangular subfascial depression situated on the anterior aspect of the elbow joint. It is bounded superiorly by an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus, medially by the pronator teres muscle, and laterally by the medial border of the brachioradialis muscle.
steps.say: The cubital fossa is a triangular depression in front of the elbow. It is bounded superiorly by a line joining the humeral epicondyles, medially by pronator teres, and laterally by the medial border of brachioradialis.

steps.tx: The roof of the cubital fossa is formed by skin, superficial fascia containing the **median cubital vein**, the medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm, and the deep investing antebrachial fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. The median cubital vein shunts blood from the cephalic to the basilic vein and is the premier site for venepuncture.
steps.say: The roof of the cubital fossa comprises skin, superficial fascia housing the median cubital vein, cutaneous nerves, and deep fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. The median cubital vein is the primary site for intravenous blood draws.

steps.tx: The floor of the cubital fossa is formed by two deep muscles: the brachialis muscle proximally and the **supinator** muscle distally wrapping around the proximal radius. The floor supports the contents of the fossa and separates them from the capsule of the elbow joint.
steps.say: The floor of the cubital fossa is formed by two muscles: brachialis in the upper portion and supinator in the lower portion. This floor cushions the deep contents against the anterior elbow joint capsule.

steps.tx: The contents of the cubital fossa arranged from medial to lateral are recalled by the classic mnemonic MBBR: the **median nerve**, the brachial artery and its bifurcation into radial and ulnar arteries, the tendon of biceps brachii, and the radial nerve deep beneath the brachioradialis margin.
steps.say: From medial to lateral, the cubital fossa contents follow the mnemonic MBBR: median nerve, brachial artery and its bifurcation, biceps brachii tendon, and the radial nerve tucked under brachioradialis.

steps.tx: The **brachial artery** bisects the cubital fossa, bifurcating opposite the neck of the radius into the radial and ulnar arteries. The bicipital aponeurosis passes superficial to the brachial artery, protecting it during emergency venepuncture of the median cubital vein, which lies directly over it in the subcutaneous tissue.
steps.say: The brachial artery bisects the fossa, dividing at the radial neck into radial and ulnar arteries. The bicipital aponeurosis covers the artery, shielding it from accidental puncture during blood draws from the median cubital vein.

steps.tx: In the anatomical position with fully extended elbow and supinated forearm, the long axis of the forearm diverges laterally from the long axis of the arm by ten to fifteen degrees in men and twenty degrees in women, known as the **carrying angle**. This lateral deviation clears the hips during walking.
steps.say: With extended elbow and supinated forearm, the forearm angles laterally from the arm by ten to fifteen degrees in men and twenty degrees in women, known as the carrying angle. This alignment clears the swinging forearm past the hips during walking.

steps.tx: Malunion of a paediatric supracondylar fracture causes medial deviation of the forearm, termed cubitus varus or gunstock deformity. Conversely, an exaggerated carrying angle exceeding twenty degrees constitutes **cubitus valgus**, which stretches the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle, producing tardy ulnar nerve palsy years after childhood injury.
steps.say: Malunion of a supracondylar fracture leads to cubitus varus, or gunstock deformity. Conversely, an exaggerated carrying angle over twenty degrees is cubitus valgus, which stretches the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle to cause delayed ulnar palsy.

steps.tx: The head of the radius is encircled by the fibro-osseous **annular ligament**, which lines with articular cartilage to cup the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna. In toddlers aged one to four, sudden longitudinal traction pulling on an extended, pronated hand causes subluxation of the radial head out of the annular ligament, known as nursemaid elbow.
steps.say: The radial head is collared by the annular ligament, keeping it seated against the ulna. In toddlers, sudden upward traction on a pronated arm slips the immature radial head out from beneath the ligament, producing nursemaid elbow.
